source: Cook, Goodman, Schulz (2011) Where science starts: spontaneous experiments in preschoolers' exploratory play
finding: Experiment 1 design: 60 preschoolers learned a base rate (all beads, or some beads, activate a machine). Then they saw a stuck pair of beads activate it and played alone. Only the Some Beads children had ambiguous evidence about which bead was causal.
numbers: N=60, mean age 54 months (range 46-64), 3 groups of 20: All Beads, Some Beads B, Some Beads AB. Warm-up play time and action counts did not differ (F(2,25)=1.38 ns; F(2,25)=.24 ns).
limits: Single lab, one toy. The base rate carried the ambiguity, so the result shows sensitivity to prior plus affordance, not a general habit.
agent_relevance: The cue for an informative test was a mismatch between prior and observation. A scaffold can compute that mismatch in code instead of asking the model.

source: Cook, Goodman, Schulz (2011) Where science starts: spontaneous experiments in preschoolers' exploratory play
finding: Experiment 1 result: few children split the bead pair in the All Beads condition, about half did in the Some Beads conditions. The informative test was rare when evidence was unambiguous.
numbers: All Beads 1 of 20 (5%) tested each bead separately; Some Beads B 9 of 20 (45%); Some Beads AB 10 of 20 (50%). Chi2(1,N=40)=8.53 and 10.16, both p<.005 vs All Beads. B vs AB: chi2=0.10 ns. In All Beads 65% never pulled the pair apart. Coder agreement 95% (kappa .90).
quote: Only one child (5%) in the All Beads condition performed the informative experiment.
limits: Even in the best condition about half of children did NOT run the test. The effect is a shift in rate, not an all-or-none switch. The success criterion was strict (both beads tested separately).
agent_relevance: Expect a scaffold to raise the rate of the discriminating test, not make it certain. Add a forced S7 check for when the signal fires.

source: Cook, Goodman, Schulz (2011) Where science starts: spontaneous experiments in preschoolers' exploratory play
finding: Key control: ambiguous evidence did not make children play more broadly. It made them do the one critical action. This rules out the simple account that uncertainty raises general exploration.
numbers: Number of action categories about 3.8 across conditions, F(2,60)=1.08 ns (Exp 1); Exp 2 t(40)=0.89 ns (about 3.00 in Some Beads). Only the snapped-apart-pair action differed: 63% vs 18% (chi2(1,N=40)=9.37, p<.005). Other actions: ns.
limits: Free play was a coarse count of 7 mutually exclusive categories. A footnote says the nulls on other actions were tested one-tailed on purpose, a lenient choice for a no-difference claim.
agent_relevance: Open-mode S3 (broad exploring) and S7 (targeted discriminating test) are different. Uncertainty should trigger S7 selection, not only more S3 sampling.

source: Cook, Goodman, Schulz (2011) Where science starts: spontaneous experiments in preschoolers' exploratory play
finding: Experiment 2: children invented a new intervention. They held a stuck bead pair vertically so only one bead touched the machine, to isolate which bead caused the effect. This action was not in the usual play repertoire.
numbers: N=40, mean age 54 months (range 48-63), 20 per condition. All Beads 1 of 20 (5%) vs Some Beads 9 of 20 (45%) tested one bead at a time; chi2(1,N=40)=8.53, p<.005. Coder agreement 96% for first coding; 86% (kappa .71) on play categories.
limits: Same effect size as Exp 1, same lab. Not an independent replication. Exp 2 was prompted by a chance observation in pilot, so it follows up a post-hoc idea.
agent_relevance: Shows design of a new test (not only choice from a menu). Supports an operator that proposes a new test when none is on the list.

source: Cook, Goodman, Schulz (2011) Where science starts: spontaneous experiments in preschoolers' exploratory play
finding: Authors say what is not shown: the study cannot tell whether children knew from the start that isolating variables helps, or inferred it during the session. Children's beliefs about contact causality were also wrong about the real mechanism.
quote: This study does not establish however, whether children understood the importance of isolating variables initially or whether they inferred its importance...
limits: Open question on competence versus on-the-spot inference. No test of whether the test led to a correct belief afterwards.
agent_relevance: Do not credit the scaffold with understanding. Check that the discriminating test is used to update the belief (G2, G3).

source: Gweon & Schulz (2008) Stretching to learn: ambiguous evidence and variability in preschoolers' exploratory play
finding: Earlier version of the effect. After confounded evidence, children played on the inconvenient far side of a mat. After unconfounded evidence, they stayed on the near, easy side.
numbers: N=32 (16 per condition). Mat usage ratio higher on the closer side in Unconfounded: t(30)=2.57, p<.02. Preferred closer side: 10 of 16 Unconfounded vs 2 of 16 Confounded; chi2(1,N=32)=8.53, p<.003. Total play time 52.19 vs 52.75 s (t(30)=0.16 ns). In Confounded, 7 of 16 (44%) tried each block on each side.
limits: Cost of play was movement effort, not time. The authors say two readings stay open: less variable play when unambiguous, or more variable play when confounded. Conference paper, small N.
agent_relevance: Shows the effect holds at a cost: children pay effort to disambiguate. A budget rule should pay for a test only when ambiguity is real.

source: Schulz & Bonawitz (2007) Serious fun: preschoolers engage in more exploratory play when evidence is confounded
finding: Described in the opened Gweon and Schulz paper: with a two-lever box, confounded evidence (both levers pushed together) led children to override a novelty preference and play with the familiar toy. Unconfounded evidence led to novelty-seeking at the new toy.
numbers: Numbers not read this session.
limits: Secondhand from b06; not opened. N and effect sizes unverified.
agent_relevance: Ambiguity can beat novelty. Open-mode rule: if a live ambiguity exists, resolve it before moving to new items.

source: Bonawitz, Shafto, Gweon, Goodman, Spelke, Schulz (2011) The double-edged sword of pedagogy
finding: Boundary condition: when an adult teaches one function of a toy, children explore less and find fewer other functions. Instruction narrows search. Same Cognition issue and lab as Cook et al.
numbers: Exp 1 N=85 preschoolers. Play time Pedagogical 119.2 s vs Interrupted 179.6, Naive 132.7, Baseline 205.7 (F(1,81)=4.52, p<.05). Kinds of actions 4.00 vs 5.30, 5.90, 6.15 (F(1,81)=9.39, p<.01). First 60 s: 3.16 vs 3.75, 4.90, 4.15 (F(1,81)=7.18, p<.05). Exp 2 N=64 (mean age 61 months): share of play on the shown function Direct 52%, Indirect Child 60%, Indirect Adult 37%.
limits: One toy with several hidden functions. Cells of about 20. Not a replication of Cook, but the same lab's exploration measures move with who gives the information.
agent_relevance: A prompt that states a hypothesis can act like pedagogy and shrink exploration. Keep the open-mode S3 prompt free of a suggested answer (consistent with G4, G5).

source: Siegel, Magid, Pelz, Tenenbaum, Schulz (2021) Children's exploratory play tracks the discriminability of hypotheses
finding: Large extension: children's exploration time follows how hard it is to tell two hypotheses apart, in a graded way, across 16 contrasts. Time is independent of the true content of the box.
numbers: N=160 children (mean 5;4) in 7 experiments. Exploration time vs discriminability: beta=0.24 (95% CI .18-.30); model correlation r=0.95 (video coding) and r=0.89 (motion sensor). Exploration vs number of marbles actually in the box: beta=0.0065 (CI -.0094 to .022). Trial order: beta=-0.051. Age effect on hard vs easy: beta=-0.041 (CI -.45 to .40).
limits: Perceptual (sound) task with marble-count contrasts, aggregated across conditions, so a high r is partly from averaging. Ages 4-8 only. Shows graded sensitivity, not the Cook bead task.
agent_relevance: Gives a dose-response rule: spend more tests when the gap between candidate answers is small. The program can compute a discriminability score and set the test budget from it.

source: Kosoy, Liu, Collins, Chan, Hamrick, Ke, Huang, Kaufmann, Canny, Gopnik (2022) Learning causal overhypotheses through exploration in children and computational models
finding: Boundary: when children get no cue about the hypothesis space (not-given condition), they explore but often fail to collect enough data to settle the rule. Giving the hypothesis space raised data sufficiency.
numbers: N=85 children aged 4-5 (20-23 per condition, 2x2 conjunctive/disjunctive x given/not given hypothesis). Enough data to settle: 71% Given vs 32% Not Given (p=0.002, 2-proportion z). Mean actions 14.07 (178.65 s) Given vs 10.58 (195.38 s) Not Given. Empty-machine test by 17.7% and 17.5%; reordered same set by 66.7% and 65%.
quote: without guidance, children may explore unbounded sets of overhypotheses, which may not be useful for discriminating
limits: Online museum study. Children's play matched neither simple info-gain nor reward models. Children repeated tests and reordered objects, so much play was not information-efficient.
agent_relevance: Unguided exploration is wide and wasteful. A named hypothesis set (from S2/S3) makes the S7 test more likely to be sufficient. Fits the scaffold: code holds the candidate list.

source: Kosoy et al. (2022) as above - RL and ideal-observer comparison
finding: Authors conclude that information-gain-optimal agents explore differently from children in the same causal environment. Children's exploration reflected neither plain overhypothesis information gain nor reward maximisation.
numbers: Children N=85 vs ideal-observer and RL baselines in the same web environment (agent returns not extracted).
limits: Not LLMs: simple ideal-observer and RL baselines. The gap may reflect the baselines chosen.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a pure info-gain objective gives child-like behaviour; children also hold broad rival hypotheses.

source: Samiei, Yiu, GX-Chen, Lin, Shen, Richards, Gopnik, Precup (2026) Human adults and LLMs as scientists: who benefits from active exploration?
finding: Active exploration removes the adult conjunctive handicap seen in passive tasks, but only when choice and outcome are coupled. Six LLMs at temperature 0 get the same task.
numbers: Humans: 306 adults on Prolific (102 Active, 102 Passive Observers, rest Passive Proposers). Conjunctive object ID: Active Explorer 0.69, Passive Observer 0.45, Passive Proposer 0.12. Rule choice: 0.82 vs 0.69 vs 0.57. LLMs: 6 models, 24 trials per rule type (288 trials in total).
limits: Cites Cook et al. (2011) only as background. Adults, not preschoolers; the nexiom task is a blicket variant; CogSci 2026 paper, so far unreplicated. Small design: 6 configurations x 4 repeats per model.
agent_relevance: Proposing tests without seeing your own outcomes is as bad as or worse than passive viewing. The program should run the test and feed the real output back to the same slot (G2).

source: Samiei et al. (2026) - exploration effort table
finding: LLMs run about as many tests as humans but search less efficiently, and conjunctive rules need more tests than disjunctive for every agent.
numbers: Tests, conjunctive/disjunctive: avg human 9.6/6.4; top human 8.5/3.8; gpt-5 10.2/7.7; gpt-5-mini 10.8/7.1; gemini-2.5-flash 13.5/9.71; deepseek-reasoner 8.2/6.8; o4-mini 6.7/4.2; deepseek-chat 12.3/11.9. gpt-5 and deepseek-reasoner reach near-perfect disjunctive accuracy; deepseek-chat and o4-mini are only modestly above baseline in conjunctive; even gpt-5 stays below top humans.
quote: LLMs do not consistently gain from choosing their own interventions
limits: Per-model conjunctive accuracies are in a figure and were not extracted. Time per test differs by up to 7x, so effort is not comparable across rows.
agent_relevance: Fewer tests (o4-mini) was not better. Test count is the wrong target; the right target is whether each test splits the live hypotheses.

source: Piriyakulkij, Langenfeld, Le, Ellis (2024) Doing experiments and revising rules with natural language and probabilistic reasoning
finding: An LLM proposes natural-language rules; Monte Carlo inference updates beliefs; experiments are picked by information gain. It beats a ReAct-style LLM agent on a Zendo task and fits human accuracy.
numbers: Human accuracy 5.26/8; ReAct agent 4.60/8; fuzzy-rule model 5.35/8; strongest model 6.55/8. Fit to human fine-grained accuracy: fuzzy online R2=.57, hard-rule R2=.10, batch R2=.05; LLM alone R2=.13. Majority-red rule learned 30-40% of the time by both humans and the model.
limits: Zendo-style rule task, not child play; small online human sample. The model is hand-built around information gain, so it supports the method, not that an LLM alone explores well.
agent_relevance: Closest working analogue of S7 in code: the program scores candidate tests by expected information gain over live hypotheses. The LLM alone (R2=.13 to humans) was worse.

source: Lidayan, Du, Kosoy, Rufova, Abbeel, Gopnik (2025) Intrinsically-motivated humans and agents in open-world exploration
finding: In Crafter, adults, children and RL agents were compared. Entropy and Empowerment tracked human exploration progress; Information Gain did not consistently. Children's goal talk related to exploration scores.
numbers: Children's breadth-depth correlation rho=0.51 (p=0.01), adults rho=-0.27 (p=0.21). Fraction of goal utterances vs exploration score rho=0.8 (p=0.005, unadjusted) in children only; none for adults or for questions. Child sample 26 children aged 8+.
limits: Small child sample, many tests, unadjusted p. Open-world game, not spontaneous experiments. RL agents, not LLMs. Information gain was weaker in a large state space, unlike small hypothesis sets.
agent_relevance: Information gain suits closed hypothesis sets (S7); in open worlds (S3) a diversity or control signal may serve better. Two different selectors.

source: Kosoy et al. (2020) Exploring exploration: comparing children with RL agents in unified environments
finding: Children in a DeepMind Lab maze: how much they explored with no goal predicted how fast they later found a goal. Search followed depth-first more closely with a goal.
numbers: Free exploration covered 22% (low), 44% (medium), 71% (high) of the maze. Steps to goal: 95, 89, 66. Choices consistent with depth-first search: 89.61% no-goal vs 96.04% goal (p=0.0073).
limits: Workshop paper, preliminary, sample size not extracted. Not the ambiguity effect.
agent_relevance: Free exploration pays off later: supports a short open-mode S3 before a task, as a preliminary result only.

source: Yiu, Allen, Ginosar, Gopnik (2025) Empowerment gain and causal model construction
finding: Proposes empowerment (control over outcomes) as a link between causal learning and RL, with a child and adult study. Notes that LLMs have limited causal learning and cites Kosoy 2022 for it.
numbers: Study numbers not extracted.
limits: Opened for context only; I did not read the empirical section.
agent_relevance: Background for an ambiguity-or-control trigger. Low weight.

source: Cook et al. (2011) - replication status
finding: I found no direct replication or failed replication of the bead-isolation result in this session. Search quota ran out partway. Closest support is conceptual: Gweon & Schulz 2008 (earlier), Siegel 2021 (graded dose-response), Kosoy 2022 (hypothesis space matters).
numbers: 0 direct replications found. Original: 2 experiments, N=60 and N=40, one lab.
limits: Absence of evidence only. A registered replication or a ManyBabies-style study may exist and was not searched for. Treat the effect size as unreplicated.
agent_relevance: Rate this as single-lab, not [E]. Test it on the model itself (own measurement) before relying on it.

source: Bonawitz, van Schijndel, Friel, Schulz (2012) Children balance theories and evidence in exploration, explanation, and learning
finding: Not opened. Recalled from memory as showing that children's exploration depends on both prior theory and evidence.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Cited from memory; details unverified. Do not use as evidence until opened.
agent_relevance: Possible source for an anomaly-drives-test rule; verify first.

source: Schulz, Gopnik, Glymour (2007) Preschool children learn about causal structure from conditional interventions
finding: Not opened. Cited in Samiei 2026 for the claim that children learn more effectively when they design their own tests.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Secondhand only.
agent_relevance: Backs the point that the learner should own the test and its outcome (see b12).

source: Chen & Klahr (1999) All other things being equal: acquisition and transfer of the control-of-variables strategy
finding: Not opened. In the Gweon and Schulz reference list, cited for the view that children are poor at designing controlled tests on their own, which makes Cook's spontaneous isolation notable.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Different tasks (school-age, explicit experiment design). Do not mix with preschool play.
agent_relevance: Contrast: unprompted isolation in play versus explicit controlled design. A scaffold should prompt the isolation step rather than hope for it.

source: Competing explanations for the Cook effect
finding: Three rival readings remain after the opened papers. (1) Expected information gain over base rate and affordances (the authors' account). (2) Cheap trial and error that happens to isolate a bead in Some Beads children. (3) Children learn within the session that isolation is useful. The discriminating experiments have not been done.
numbers: Cook 2011 did not separate them; Gweon & Schulz 2008 list a similar pair (less variable when unambiguous vs more variable when confounded).
limits: Drawn from Cook, Gweon & Schulz and Siegel. No paper found that runs the direct test (for example giving the informative action for free, or training in isolation first).
agent_relevance: A scaffold that always runs the isolating test costs little and does not depend on which account is right.

source: Moderators across the opened papers
finding: Moderators with numbers: who gives the evidence (teaching cut other-function play: Bonawitz 2011); hypothesis space given or not (71% vs 32% sufficient data: Kosoy 2022); owning the outcome (0.69 vs 0.12: Samiei 2026); age (no age effect on hard-contrast preference in 4-8 year olds: Siegel 2021).
limits: Cross-paper summary. No culture, expertise or time-pressure moderators found in the papers I opened.
agent_relevance: Our controllable moderators: no suggested answer in the prompt, a stated candidate set, and the same slot sees its own test result.

source: LLM coverage of the Cook contrast: what is missing
finding: I found no LLM study that reproduces the Cook ambiguous versus unambiguous contrast directly (base-rate manipulation, measure of whether the model picks the isolating action). The 2022-2026 LLM work uses blicket-style or Zendo-style tasks.
numbers: Checked: Samiei 2026, Piriyakulkij 2024, Kosoy 2022 reference lists. arXiv API title queries for blicket returned nothing in this session, so the sweep is incomplete.
limits: Incomplete: web search quota ran out and arXiv API queries returned empty. A GX-Chen 2025 LLM blicket study is cited but I could not open it.
agent_relevance: A gap we can fill with our own test: a base-rate ambiguity manipulation on the model, measuring the rate of the isolating action.

source: Siegel et al. 2021 - trial effects and individual variation
finding: Exploration dropped only slightly over four trials. Hardest contrasts were explored longer than the easiest regardless of age.
numbers: Trial effect beta=-0.051 (CI -.086 to -.016); accuracy rose with discriminability beta=1.12 (CI .64-1.46); age effect on accuracy beta=0.033 (CI -.0074 to .069, marginal).
limits: Same sample as b09. Children first showed in forced-choice tasks that they could tell the hypotheses apart.
agent_relevance: Supports a test budget that scales with ambiguity and stays steady across repeated items.

source: Cook et al. (2011) - what ambiguous means in the design
finding: Ambiguity was made by two things together: the base rate (some beads do not work) and a stuck pair whose members cannot be told apart. All Beads children saw the same stuck pair activate, but a prior that all beads work left nothing to learn.
numbers: Same stuck-pair demonstration produced 5% vs 45-50% informative tests.
limits: Ambiguity and expected gain are confounded with the number of possibly non-working beads. A design that keeps ambiguity but removes expected gain was not run.
agent_relevance: Trigger S7 on 'candidate causes remain AND a test could split them', not on 'unsure' alone.
